subtitle: Master the harmonic patterns that drive all popular music
heroDescription: Chord progressions are sequences of chords that create the harmonic foundation of music. They provide the emotional journey, structural framework, and stylistic character that defines every song. Master progressions to understand how harmony works and create compelling musical experiences.

whatAreProgressions.title: What Are Chord Progressions?
whatAreProgressions.description: A chord progression is a sequence of chords played in succession that creates the harmonic foundation of a piece of music. Progressions establish key centers, create emotional movement, and provide the structure that supports melody and rhythm. Understanding progressions is essential because they control:

progressionTypes.name: I-IV-V
progressionTypes.description: The foundational progression in Western music. Used in rock, pop, country, and blues.

progressionTypes.name: ii-V-I
progressionTypes.description: The cornerstone of jazz harmony. Creates smooth voice leading and strong resolution.

progressionTypes.name: I-V-vi-IV
progressionTypes.description: The "axis progression" found in countless pop hits across all decades.

progressionTypes.name: 12 Bar Blues
progressionTypes.description: The backbone of blues, R&B, and early rock & roll. A must-know for all guitarists.

progressionTypes.name: vi-IV-I-V
progressionTypes.description: Popular in modern pop and alternative rock. Creates emotional tension and release.

progressionTypes.name: Circle of Fifths
progressionTypes.description: Advanced harmonic movement. Essential for jazz and classical music.

progressionTypes.name: I-IV
progressionTypes.description: The two-chord subdominant shuttle. A gentle rocking motion used in folk, gospel, and rock anthems.

progressionTypes.name: IV-I Plagal
progressionTypes.description: The 'Amen cadence' — a soft, peaceful resolution from subdominant to tonic used in hymns and gospel.

progressionTypes.name: I-V
progressionTypes.description: The simplest tension-resolution pair. Two chords that drive punk, folk, and countless singalongs.

progressionTypes.name: I-bVII-IV
progressionTypes.description: The Mixolydian vamp. A modal rock progression with a bluesy, rootsy character.

progressionTypes.name: I-vi-ii-V
progressionTypes.description: The jazz turnaround. Smooth circle-of-fifths motion used in standards and doo-wop.

progressionTypes.name: I-vi-IV-V
progressionTypes.description: The '50s doo-wop progression. The sound of early rock & roll and timeless ballads.

progressionTypes.name: Minor Blues
progressionTypes.description: The darker side of the blues. A 12-bar form in minor keys for intense, moody expression.

progressionTypes.name: I-bIII-bVII-IV
progressionTypes.description: Modal rock with borrowed chords. The sound of classic rock, grunge, and Britpop anthems.

progressionTypes.name: I-V-bVII-IV
progressionTypes.description: The rock anthem progression. Combines dominant power with modal rebellion for arena-sized sound.

progressionTypes.name: ii-IV-V
progressionTypes.description: The country turnaround. Stepwise pre-dominant chain common in Nashville songwriting.

romanNumerals.description: Musicians use Roman numerals to describe chord progressions regardless of key. This system makes it easy to transpose progressions and understand harmonic function across different musical contexts.
